Title: Defect detection in EBSM components through selective box fusion of modern object detection
Text:
Defect detection in EBSM 
components through selective box 
fusion of modern object detection
Rui Han1, Chenwei Wang1, Yuzhong Wang1, Yihui Zhang1, Wenhua Guo1, Yanyang Zi1 & 
Jiyuan Zhao2
Additive Manufacturing (AM) technology has gained widespread application across various industries 
due to its capability to directly produce products from computer-aided design models. Among AM 
techniques, the Electron Beam Selective Melting (EBSM) process has attracted significant attention, 
particularly in aerospace and automotive industries, owing to its high precision, speed, and excellent 
material properties. However, various defects, especially internal defects that inevitably arise 
during the manufacturing process, significantly limit the performance of EBSM parts. In this study, 
X-ray computed tomography (CT) was utilized to scan EBSM parts, and cross-sectional images were 
employed to train several state-of-the-art modern object detection models for evaluating their 
effectiveness in detecting internal defects. Sparse R-CNN demonstrated the best overall performance, 
while the YOLO series excelled in specific metrics. To further capitalize on the strengths of different 
detection models, a model ensemble approach, Selective Box Fusion (SBF) is proposed. This approach 
employs voting and weighted fusion of detection boxes to mitigate errors inherent in individual 
models. Experimental results show that the SBF ensemble method effectively integrates the 
advantages of multiple detection models, leading to improvements across various evaluation metrics 
compared to individual models and other ensemble methods.
Keywords  Additive manufacturing, Electron beam selective melting, Computed tomography, Defect 
detection, Model ensemble
In recent years, additive manufacturing (AM) technology has attracted significant attention due to its ability to 
rapidly produce complex structures and functional components1,2. AM holds promising applications in fields 
such as automotive industry, aerospace, and medical devices3. Among the various AM processes, Electron 
Beam Selective Melting (EBSM) is distinguished by its high precision, speed, and superior material properties4. 
However, like traditional manufacturing techniques, the EBSM process inevitably introduces defects5, including 
pores, cracks, and lack of fusion (LOF). These defects not only compromise the mechanical performance of parts 
but also pose potential safety risks6.
Detecting defects in EBSM components is therefore essential for ensuring quality control and optimizing 
the manufacturing process. Currently, various non-destructive testing (NDT) techniques have been employed 
to inspect AM components7, with industrial computed tomography (CT) gaining significant attention due 
to its high precision in detecting internal defects. Traditional manual inspection methods, however, are 
time-consuming, labor-intensive, and inefficient, making them inadequate for high-speed and high-quality 
production in industrial settings. As a result, researchers have turned to machine learning methods to achieve 
automated and intelligent defect detection8,9. While conventional machine learning approaches such as Support 
Vector Machines (SVM) and Decision Trees (DT) have been widely utilized, deep learning techniques have seen 
limited application in this domain. Defect detection is inherently related to object detection, which involves 
identifying and accurately locating targets within an image. Recently, modern object detection methods based on 
deep learning have achieved significant progress10, leading to the development of various powerful techniques. 
Despite their success in general object detection tasks, their full potential remains underexplored in the context 
of defect detection.
The complex internal structures and varying material properties of EBSM components make internal defect 
detection particularly challenging. Hence, leveraging modern object detection methods for automated internal

defect detection is an important area of research. In this study, industrial CT scans of EBSM components were 
performed, and several modern object detection methods were employed to identify internal defects in the 
resulting CT cross-sectional images. Through experiments, the detection performance of these methods was 
evaluated. To further improve detection performance, we propose a model ensemble method, Selective Box 
Fusion (SBF), which was validated for its effectiveness. This approach integrates the strengths of multiple deep 
learning methods, leading to enhanced accuracy and reliability in internal defect detection. Additionally, this 
study aims to offer valuable insights for researchers in AM and contribute to the advancement of this field. The 
main contributions of this study are summarized as follows:
•	 Applied modern object detection methods to detect internal defects in EBSM components using X-ray CT 
images.
•	 Evaluated the performance of modern object detection methods, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses 
in different metrics.
•	 Proposed a novel model ensemble method, Selective Box Fusion (SBF), to integrate predictions from multiple 
models and enhance detection accuracy.
•	 Demonstrated that the SBF method improves detection performance compared to individual models and 
other ensemble methods across various evaluation metrics.
Related works
Defect detection in additive manufactured components
To prevent costly failures caused by various defects, NDT technologies have been adopted and integrated into 
AM. NDT is widely used in industry to assess the quality of materials, components, structures, or systems, 
identifying faults and discontinuities without causing damage to the original parts. Various NDT methods 
employed in AM include eddy current testing, optical inspection, acoustic inspection, and industrial CT, among 
others.
Ehlers et al.11 integrated a high-spatial-resolution magnetoresistive array with a single-wire excitation coil 
to conduct eddy current testing on the surface of stainless-steel powder samples produced by laser powder bed 
fusion additive manufacturing. Guo et al.12 demonstrated the effectiveness of subsurface eddy current testing for 
defect detection, showing that the amplitude and phase angle of the eddy current signal were proportional to the 
defect size in chromium-nickel alloy 738LC samples produced by laser selective melting. Raplee et al.13 applied 
infrared imaging to study temperature distributions in the EBSM process, detecting process-related defects based 
on the resulting thermal patterns. AbouelNour et al.14 utilized both optical imaging and infrared thermography 
to detect point and line defects, comparing temperature monitoring and thermal image analysis against baseline 
conditions for defect detection. Chen et al.15 processed acoustic emission (AE) signals from the direct energy 
deposition process using two validated deep learning models: R-CED16 for speech enhancement and F-DNN17 
for speech denoising. Chabot et al. proposed an additive manufacturing defect detection method using phased 
array ultrasonic testing (PAUT), which was demonstrated to be effective for wire arc additive manufacturing 
(WAAM) components and suitable for laser metal deposition (LMD). Davis et al.18 employed laser ultrasound 
technology to detect defects in SLM-manufactured parts, comparing the results with CT scans. Babamiri et al.19 
utilized X-ray computed tomography to identify defects such as cracks, porosity, and residual powder in Inconel 
718 additive parts under both quasi-static and dynamic conditions. Bol et al.20 performed CT scans on Ti-6Al-
4V samples produced by electron beam powder bed fusion (EB-PBF), characterizing porosity and classifying 
pore features by volume, surface area, diameter, density, sphericity, spatial distribution, and orientation.
Eddy current and optical inspection methods primarily target surface or subsurface defects, while ultrasonic 
testing, though capable of detecting internal defects, often struggles with limited spatial resolution, making it 
difficult to accurately characterize defects. In contrast, CT provides high-precision, non-destructive detection 
of internal defects7, and has gained increasing attention as a prominent NDT method in AM. To meet the high-
precision internal defect detection requirements of EBSM components, this study used industrial CT scans as 
the data source for internal defect detection.
Defect detection based on deep learning
In recent years, deep learning has achieved remarkable success across a wide range of applications. As deep 
learning technologies continue to advance, their integration into defect detection methods has significantly 
enhanced detection capabilities.
Hu et al.21 improved Faster R-CNN by incorporating ResNet50, GRAPN residual units, and ShuffleNetV2 to 
detect surface defects on printed circuit boards (PCBs). Feng et al.22 employed YOLOv5 to effectively identify 
and locate insulator defects on power transmission lines, reducing the need for unsafe manual inspections and 
improving detection efficiency. Hang et al.23 proposed a lightweight, real-time defect detection network using 
MobileNetV3 as the backbone, which achieved multi-layer feature pyramid detection of surface defects on 
sanitary ceramics. Parlak et al.24 trained several state-of-the-art deep learning-based object detection models, 
including YOLOv3, YOLOv4, YOLOv5, YOLOR, EfficientDet, and RetinaNet, on an X-ray image dataset of 
high-pressure aluminum die-casting parts, successfully detecting internal defects and predicting their types 
without human intervention. Jiang et al.25 introduced a dual-channel encoding fusion decoding (DCE-FD) 
network based on the UNet architecture, which was used to detect pores, shrinkage, minor defects, and edge 
defects in radiographic images of castings.
Modern deep learning techniques have also found applications in defect detection within AM. Wong et 
al.26 used a 3D U-Net to automatically segment defects in AM parts from CT images. Wang et al.27 developed 
a defect detection model, CenterNet-CL, based on CenterNet with an hourglass backbone, to detect surface 
defects in electron scanning microscope images of additively manufactured components. Shang et al.28 proposed

fast and accurate detection of surface defects in wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) parts. Lu et al.30 
compared the performance of YOLOv4, SSD, and Faster R-CNN for detecting wear and misalignment defects 
in continuous fiber-reinforced composites during AM, using high-speed camera images. YOLOv4 was found to 
be the most effective model, providing superior accuracy and efficiency. Ahsan et al.31 utilized 11 deep learning 
models to classify the presence or absence of surface defects in AM parts, showcasing the adaptability and 
effectiveness of deep learning models in this field.
While previous research has demonstrated the feasibility and high effectiveness of using deep learning for 
defect detection, the performance of different models varies significantly across different scenarios. Therefore, 
this paper systematically evaluates the performance of modern object detection methods in detecting defects 
within EBSM components.
Modern object detection methods
Object detection is a core task in computer vision, aimed at identifying and localizing objects in images. Defect 
detection shares similarities with object detection, as it involves locating and classifying defects in parts. This 
section provides an overview of modern object detection methods, forming the basis for selecting methods to 
detect defects in EBSM components.
Object detection typically uses bounding boxes to represent the location and extent of objects, while 
specifying their categories. Earlier object detection methods were split into two categories: two-stage and single-
stage methods. Two-stage methods, also known as region-based methods, generate region proposals in the first 
phase and classify them in the second. R-CNN32 and Fast R-CNN33 popularized this approach, though early 
models used slow, computationally expensive techniques like selective search34. R-FCN35, Faster R-CNN36, and 
the more recent Sparse R-CNN37 improved speed and accuracy through faster region proposal networks and 
deep learning techniques. Single-stage methods, such as YOLO38, SSD39, and RetinaNet40, bypass the region 
proposal step by predicting bounding boxes and classes in a single pass, allowing real-time detection. The YOLO 
series, from YOLOv1 to YOLOv841, has seen consistent improvements in speed and accuracy, with YOLOv8 
featuring anchor-free detection and decoupled heads.
Transformer models42, first introduced in natural language processing, have also influenced object detection. 
Carion et al.43 applied transformers to object detection, creating the DEtection TRansformer (DETR), sparking 
the development of high-performing algorithms44–48, which are referred to in this paper as DETR-based 
methods. Among them, DINO48 further enhanced efficiency through techniques like denoising training and 
mixed query selection.
For this study, a combination of classic and modern recent object detection methods from all categories is 
selected to assess their effectiveness in detecting defects in EBSM parts.
Model ensemble
Ensembling predictions from multiple models can improve generalization and often leads to more accurate 
results than relying on a single model49. Model ensemble have consistently performed well in machine learning 
competitions50,51.
In object detection, model ensemble techniques have also gained significant traction in recent years. Angela 
et al.52 proposed an ensemble algorithm that can be applied to any object detection model, regardless of the 
underlying algorithm. Solovyev et al.53 introduced Weighted Boxes Fusion (WBF), which averages bounding 
boxes based on their confidence scores, thereby merging predictions from multiple object detection models. 
Additionally, Atakan et al.54 developed a weighted ensemble model that optimizes coefficients to combine the 
detection results of three different models trained on a remote sensing image dataset, yielding outputs that 
account for these optimized coefficients. Walambe et al.55 implemented ensemble transfer learning to boost 
baseline object detection models for multi-scale target detection in drone imagery.
While model ensemble methods have proven effective in many machine learning tasks, including object 
detection, limited research has focused on their application in defect detection, particularly for internal defects 
in EBSM components. This paper analyzes existing model ensemble approaches in object detection and proposes 
a novel ensemble method tailored to defect detection in EBSM components.
Currently, traditional methods such as X-ray CT are widely used for defect detection in EBSM, but they have 
limitations, particularly in detecting small or complex defects. Recent works have seen the application of deep 
learning models, though these works still use older methods and often rely on single models, which may not 
fully exploit the potential of modern machine learning techniques. Our work addresses this gap by proposing an 
ensemble approach, the SBF, which combines predictions from multiple modern object detection methods. This 
approach aims to enhance detection accuracy by leveraging the strengths of diverse models, thereby reducing 
the errors that a single model might produce.
In summary, while conventional methods such as CT are widely employed for defect detection in EBSM, 
they exhibit limitations, particularly in identifying small or complex defects. Recent advancements have seen the 
application of deep learning models; however, these studies often rely on older methodologies and frequently 
depend on single models, which may not fully exploit the potential of modern machine learning techniques. 
To address this gap, our work introduces the application of modern object detection methods for the detection 
of internal defects in EBSM components, evaluates their performance, and proposes a novel model ensemble 
method, termed SBF, to enhance detection performance. The SBF is designed to selectively fuse bounding boxes 
based on a voting strategy, thereby effectively integrating the strengths of multiple object detection methods.

Methodology
In this section, we first present the proposed Selective Box Fusion. We then introduce the modern object 
detection methods used for both evaluation and model ensemble in this study, followed by a description of the 
metrics used to assess the defect detection performance.
Selective box fusion
Object detection models often produce numerous predicted bounding boxes. In single-model object detection, 
techniques like Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) are typically employed to discard overlapping boxes and 
retain only the one with the highest confidence, thereby eliminating redundant predictions.
Combining predicted bounding boxes from multiple models can provide a more accurate prediction, this 
process referred to as model ensemble. Model ensemble often leads to top performance in machine learning. 
However, when using NMS-based methods in multi-model ensemble, valuable bounding boxes may be 
discarded, reducing localization accuracy and limiting overall performance. As illustrated in Figure 1 (b), when 
given a defect as shown in Figure 1 (a) and most models agree on its location, NMS-based methods retain only 
the bounding box with the highest confidence score. This may lead to suboptimal detection, as the box with the 
highest confidence may not always be the most accurate, potentially resulting in missed or incorrect detections. 
On the other hand, as illustrated in Figure 1 (f), when no defect exists but a few models incorrectly predict one, 
NMS-based methods might still retain that prediction, causing false positives.
To more effectively fuse predicted bounding boxes from various object detection models, Solovyev et al.53 
introduced the Weighted Boxes Fusion (WBF) method. WBF leverages the confidence scores of all predicted 
bounding boxes to generate a more accurate weighted average box. Compared to NMS-based methods, WBF 
utilizes the information from all predicted boxes, allowing for improved localization precision. As shown in 
Figure 1 (c), when most models correctly predict a defect, WBF averages all the predicted boxes, even if none of 
the models perfectly predict the box location, resulting in a more accurate bounding box.
However, WBF does not account for the overall accuracy of the predicted boxes. If only a few models predict 
a target while the majority do not, and no actual target exists at that location, WBF may still treat the prediction 
as valid and calculate an average box, which will reduce accuracy. As illustrated in Figure 1 (g), when no defect 
is present but a few models mistakenly predict one, WBF generates an average box, leading to a false positive.
To address the limitations of WBF, this paper proposes Selective Box Fusion (SBF), which employs a voting-
based strategy to selectively determine whether a true defect exists at a given location, based on predictions

As discussed earlier, both NMS-based methods and the WBF have a certain probability of generating 
erroneous predictions. The SBF addresses this by employing a voting strategy to selectively determine the 
validity of box clusters, thereby reducing the risk of false detections. As illustrated in Figure 1 (d), when a defect 
is truly present, and the majority of models indicate its presence, the SBF merges all predicted boxes, resulting 
in a more accurate fused box. Conversely, in scenarios where no defect is present but a minority of models still 
predict one (Figure 1 (e)), the SBF discards the corresponding box cluster (Figure 1 (h)), effectively preventing 
false detections.
Modern object detection methods used in this study
As outlined in Related Works, modern object detection methods can be broadly categorized into three 
categories: two-stage methods, one-stage methods, and DETR-based methods. In this study, two methods from 
each category were selected. These include Faster R-CNN and Sparse R-CNN from the two-stage methods, 
YOLOv5 and YOLOv8 from the one-stage methods, and DETR and DINO from the DETR-based methods. A 
brief description of each method is provided below.
Faster R-CNN
Faster R-CNN addresses the inefficiency of the selective search technique used in earlier R-CNN by introducing 
the Region Proposal Network (RPN). The RPN significantly speeds up the region proposal process by directly 
generating object proposals from the feature map in a fully convolutional manner. This innovation overcomes 
the bottleneck of traditional two-stage methods, resulting in both faster detection and improved performance. 
Faster R-CNN is thus a seminal method in object detection, representing a key advancement in balancing speed 
and performance.
Sparse R-CNN
Sparse R-CNN departs from traditional R-CNN methods, which rely on dense object proposals, by utilizing a 
fixed set of sparse learnable proposals for object classification and localization. Instead of generating numerous 
region proposals, Sparse R-CNN learns a small number of proposal boxes during training. These learnable 
proposal boxes serve as initial guesses for object locations, significantly reducing computational complexity. 
Sparse R-CNN achieves faster convergence during training while maintaining high accuracy, making it both 
computationally efficient and precise, as demonstrated in benchmark evaluations on public datasets.
YOLOv5
YOLOv5 is a single-stage object detection method that builds on the YOLO series by optimizing both speed and 
accuracy. It utilizes a backbone primarily composed of Cross Stage Partial (CSP) layers for feature extraction and 
employs a Spatial Pyramid Pooling - Fast (SPPF) layer to aggregate multi-scale features into a fixed-size feature 
map, enhancing computational efficiency. Additionally, YOLOv5 integrates an improved Path Aggregation 
Network (PAN) for effective feature processing and leverages extensive data augmentation techniques to boost 
robustness and generalization. The auto-anchor mechanism dynamically adjusts anchor sizes to better handle 
objects of varying scales. These enhancements allow YOLOv5 to offer improved detection accuracy while 
maintaining real-time performance.
YOLOv8
YOLOv8 represents the latest iteration in the YOLO series, introducing significant improvements in network 
architecture, training strategies, and inference speed. While retaining a similar structure to YOLOv5, YOLOv8 
replaces CSP layers with Faster Implementation of CSP Bottleneck with 2 convolutions (C2f) modules, which 
enhance the efficiency of feature extraction by combining high-level features with contextual information. It

adopts an anchor-free, decoupled detection head that separately handles detection, classification, and regression 
tasks, leading to improved overall performance. YOLOv8 also integrates Complete IoU (CIoU) loss and 
Distribution Focal Loss (DFL) for better bounding box regression, and a dynamic label assignment mechanism, 
which enhances model generalization by addressing label imbalance issues. These updates make YOLOv8 both 
more accurate and faster than its predecessors.
DETR
DETR (DEtection TRansformer) simplifies the object detection workflow by introducing a Transformer 
architecture, which eliminates the need for anchor boxes and post-processing. The method first extracts image 
features through a CNN, then feeds them into a Transformer encoder, which models object relationships using 
global self-attention mechanisms. The Transformer decoder predicts bounding boxes and categories in an end-
to-end manner, using a fixed-size set of object queries without predefined anchor boxes. This design significantly 
reduces handcrafted components in object detection. DETR demonstrates strong performance in detection 
tasks, particularly excelling at detecting large objects.
DINO
DINO (DETR with Improved deNoising anchOr boxes) is an enhanced version of DETR that improves 
detection accuracy and stability. DINO employs contrastive denoising training by mixing real and false anchor 
boxes, teaching the model to correct erroneous predictions and better distinguish objects. It introduces a mixed 
query selection strategy to capture multi-scale objects more effectively, reducing both missed detections and 
false positives. Additionally, DINO utilizes a “look forward twice” approach to refine parameter updates. These 
improvements optimize training speed and model stability, yielding superior performance compared to DETR.
Evaluation metrics
In object detection tasks, particularly in natural scene datasets like MS COCO56, PASCAL VOC57, and ImageNet58, 
performance is commonly evaluated using metrics such as Average Precision (AP) and Average Recall (AR). 
AP measures the proportion of correctly identified objects among all detected objects, indicating the model’s 
precision in predicting positive examples. AR represents the proportion of correctly identified objects relative 
to the total number of objects in the dataset, reflecting the model’s ability to detect all positive examples. This 
paper adopts these metrics to define the evaluation metrics for detecting internal defects in EBSM components.
To define AP and AR, it is essential to explain some key terms. The first is IoU, which quantifies the overlap 
between a predicted bounding box and the ground truth bounding box. Denote the predicted bounding box as 
bbpred and the ground truth bounding box as bbGT . The IoU is calculated as:
	
IoU = area (bbpred ∩bbGT )

compared to a predefined threshold IoUt. If the IoU exceeds IoUt, the detection is considered valid. Otherwise, 
it is deemed invalid.
Based on the above concepts, the following terms are defined:
True Positives (TP): The number of correctly detected defects, where the IoU between bbpred and bbGT  
exceeds IoUt. False Positives (FP): The number of incorrect detections, where the IoU between bbpred and bbGT  
is below IoUt, but the defect is predicted as a positive case. False Negatives (FN): The number of missed defects, 
where a bbGT  exists, but the model fails to predict a corresponding bounding box. True Negatives (TN): The 
number of correctly identified non-defects. Since there are infinitely many non-defective regions, this metric is 
typically disregarded in defect detection tasks.

AR is calculated by determining the maximum Re for various IoU thresholds and averaging these values.
In most object detection tasks, multiple categories must be detected. The mean Average Precision (mAP) 
is the mean of AP values across all categories, while the mean Average Recall (mAR) is the mean of AR values 
across all categories.
In practical applications, evaluation metrics are typically computed separately for different object categories, 
sizes, and IoU thresholds to comprehensively assess model performance. In this study, AP and mAR are 
calculated for different defect categories (including crack, LOF, and pore) to evaluate the methods’ ability to 
detect various defect types. Additionally, mAP and mAR are computed for defects of varying sizes: small defects 
(area < 32 × 32 pixels), medium defects (area between 32 × 32 and 96 × 96 pixels), and large defects (area >

Experiments and results
Defect detection dataset for EBSM components
Data acquisition
In this study, a total of 9 specimens were fabricated using the EBSM process, with the Arcam A2X system. The 
test specimens were fabricated using M247 powder, with the specific process parameters provided in Table 1. The 
produced samples are shown in Figure 3. Subsequent CT scans reveal numerous internal defects.
A GE phoenix v|tome|x m microfocus CT system was employed to scan the samples and obtain cross-
sectional images. After scanning and reconstruction, the defective regions of the samples were examined, and 
cross-sectional images were acquired from the regions containing defects.
Dataset creation
The acquired cross-sectional images were annotated with bounding boxes and categorized using LabelImg. The 
defect categories included cracks, LOF, and pore. Cracks are a typical defect in metal AM components and 
significantly degrade the material’s mechanical properties. In cross-sectional images, cracks appear as slender, 
straight, or curved lines. LOF refers to the incomplete melting of powder or insufficient overlap of molten metal 
during the manufacturing process, and in cross-sectional images, LOF typically appear as irregularly shaped, 
larger regions. Pores are usually caused by trapped gas in the molten pool and appear in cross-sectional images 
as smooth-edged, round, or pear-shaped defects, usually smaller than 100 µm.
A total of 350 cross-sectional images containing defects were collected for this study. Experts in CT inspection 
annotated 1,646 defects based on their experience. The number of defects in each category is shown in Table 2. 
Surface defects were not included in this study, as they can easily be identified through visual inspection without 
the need for CT scanning.

Experimental setup
The dataset was divided into 70% for training, 20% for validation, and 10% for testing. Six modern object 
detection methods were adapted for this study: Faster R-CNN, Sparse R-CNN, YOLOv5, YOLOv8, DETR, and 
DINO. To minimize the impact of model parameters and computational complexity on performance, ResNet-50 
was utilized as the backbone for Faster R-CNN, Sparse R-CNN, DETR, and DINO. For YOLOv5 and YOLOv8, 
the larger variants, YOLOv5l and YOLOv8l, were employed. The parameters and computational complexities 
(measured in Floating Point Operations Per Second (FLOPs)) of these models are summarized in Table 3, 
indicating that their parameter sizes are relatively comparable.
All models were implemented in Python (version: 3.9.18) using PyTorch (version: 1.13.1). Faster R-CNN, 
Sparse R-CNN, DETR, and DINO were implemented using MMDetection59 (version: 3.3.0), while YOLOv5 
and YOLOv8 utilized MMYOLO60 (version: 0.6.0). Training was conducted on four Nvidia GeForce RTX 3090 
GPUs (CUDA version: 11.7), with additional hardware comprising 256 GB RAM and an Intel® Xeon® Gold 6226R 
processor.
A comprehensive hyperparameter search was conducted using Grid Search for each model independently, 
exploring various learning rates, batch sizes, optimizers, and data augmentation strategies. The search space 
was defined based on preliminary experiments and recommendations from the methods’ original papers. For 
instance, learning rates were tested within a range of 1e-5 to 1e-3, while batch sizes were chosen considering 
GPU memory constraints.

their efficacy. Sparse R-CNN benefits from a more advanced model design and a two-stage detection strategy, 
leading to its superior performance compared to Faster R-CNN, despite both being RCNN-based. YOLOv5 and 
YOLOv8 achieved comparable results due to their similar architectures and the extensive data augmentation 
applied during training, contributing to their strong performance.
For mAP.75, YOLOv8 achieved the best results, followed closely by YOLOv5. DINO and Sparse R-CNN 
ranked next, while Faster R-CNN and DETR performed the worst. The YOLOs benefited from the application 
of the PAN, which more effectively leveraged both contextual and local image information, resulting in better 
performance on this metric. In contrast, the performance of Faster R-CNN and DETR was likely hindered by the 
limited dataset size, leading to insufficient learning in defect localization.
Next, we evaluate the performance of the methods across different categories in terms of AP. For cracks, 
YOLOv5 demonstrated the highest precision, with minimal variation among the other methods. In the case of 
LOF, YOLOv5 again achieved the best results, followed by YOLOv8, with other methods showing only slight 
differences, except for DETR, which performed the worst. For pores, Sparse R-CNN delivered outstanding 
performance, with YOLOv8 and DINO following, while Faster R-CNN and DETR lagged behind. The superior 
performance of YOLOv5 can be attributed to the Auto Anchor, which enabled better initialization of anchor 
boxes. Since cracks and LOFs tend to have consistent shapes, YOLOv5 achieved higher precision for these 
defects. On the other hand, the exceptional performance of Sparse R-CNN for pores could be explained by the 
relatively regular distribution of pores in the specimens. The learnable proposal boxes of Sparse R-CNN likely 
captured statistical patterns of pore locations, leading to its success in this category.
In terms of mAP across varying defect sizes, Sparse R-CNN performed best for small defects, followed 
by YOLOv5, with other methods showing similar results except for DETR, which performed the worst. For 
medium-sized defects, YOLOv5 performed the best, while YOLOv8 excelled in detecting large defects, with no 
significant differences among the other methods. Sparse R-CNN’s superior performance on small defects is likely 
due to the fact that most small defects are pores, while cracks and LOFs typically span larger areas. This also 
explains why the YOLOs excel in detecting medium and large objects.
Regarding recall, the overall performance was similar to precision, with Sparse R-CNN showing the best 
overall results. Specifically, Sparse R-CNN exhibited the highest performance in mAR, with YOLOv5 and 
YOLOv8 also performing well. For mARcrack, Sparse R-CNN again led, followed by YOLOv5 and YOLOv8. 
Similarly, for mARpore and mARLOF, Sparse R-CNN demonstrated superior performance. In terms of mARsmall, 
both Sparse R-CNN and YOLOv5 performed well. For mARmedium, Sparse R-CNN, YOLOv5, and YOLOv8 
showed comparable results, while YOLOv8 performed best in mARlarge, with no significant differences among 
the other methods.
Based on these results, model selection for defect detection and quality control in EBSM should be guided by 
specific detection and quality requirements: 
	1.	 If both precision and recall are critical without other specific requirements, Sparse R-CNN is the best choice.
	2.	 For high precision in defect localization and size estimation, YOLOv8 is recommended.
	3.	 To prioritize precision in detecting cracks or LOF, YOLOv5 is the preferred option.
	4.	 For crack and LOF detection where minimizing missed defects is crucial, Sparse R-CNN performs the best.
	5.	 For detecting pores and small defects, Sparse R-CNN offers the best performance.
	6.	 When detecting medium to large defects, the YOLOs offer higher precision, while Sparse R-CNN excels in 
recall.

The radar chart summarizing the evaluation results is presented in Figure 6. Based on the analysis, Sparse 
R-CNN demonstrates the best overall performance among the individual methods. Although DETR-based 
methods have shown promising results on public datasets, their performance in this study was suboptimal, due 
to the need for larger-scale datasets for effective training. On relatively smaller datasets, such as the one used 
in this study, the learnable proposal boxes allow Sparse R-CNN to better adapt, providing a clear advantage. 
The YOLOs, while constrained by their single-stage design, excel in certain metrics and maintain solid overall 
performance. Meanwhile, Faster R-CNN, despite being a widely adopted object detection method, is limited by 
its older network architecture, leading to comparatively weaker results in this study.
Comparison of ensemble methods
According to previous research52, ensembling a few high-performing models is more effective than ensembling 
all models, as including poorly performing models can introduce errors that degrade overall performance. This 
is due to the fact that less effective models contribute to incorrect decisions, which negatively impacts the overall 
results of ensemble.
Based on the analysis in Comparison of Modern Object Detection Methods, DETR and Faster R-CNN 
exhibited relatively poor performance and were therefore excluded from the ensemble. The methods that 
performed well-Sparse R-CNN, YOLOv5, YOLOv8, and DINO-were selected for the ensemble, using the 
proposed SBF and WBF for comparsion. The evaluation results of SBF and WBF are shown in the last two 
columns of Table 4, where significant improvements can be observed across most evaluation metrics. Notably, 
for mAP.50, the SBF achieved a 3% improvement over the best-performing individual method. For crack and 
LOF defects, the AP of the SBF improved by approximately 1%, and for medium and large defects, it improved 
by around 2%. However, since Sparse R-CNN was the only best-performing model for small defects and pores, 
these categories did not benefit as much from the ensemble. These results are also reflected in the radar chart in 
Figure 6.
The SBF outperformed the WBF across all evaluation metrics, with the most significant improvements 
observed in mAP.50, mAP.75, and mAPlarge. The SBF achieved a 1.8% improvement in mAP.50 over the WBF, 
indicating the effectiveness of the SBF. Since the WBF simply averages the bounding boxes from different 
models, it may include incorrect predictions, leading to suboptimal results. In contrast, the SBF employs a voting 
strategy to select valid predictions, ensuring that only accurate bounding boxes are included in the ensemble. 
This approach enhances the overall performance of the ensemble, as demonstrated by the results.
Figure 7 shows the precision-recall curve of the SBF, WBF, and individual methods. The SBF consistently 
outperforms the WBF and individual methods across different recall levels, indicating its superior performance 
in defect detection. The SBF’s precision-recall curve is closer to the upper right corner, demonstrating its ability 
to achieve higher precision without sacrificing recall. This is particularly evident in the high-recall region, where 
the SBF maintains a higher precision than the WBF and individual methods.

the weighted fusion of bounding boxes, the SBF achieved more precisive defect detection results than the WBF, 
demonstrating its superior performance in defect detection.
In terms of computational efficiency, the SBF and WBF were compared in terms of runtime and resource 
usage, as shown in Table 5. The runtime of the SBF was slightly longer than that of the WBF, with an average 
of 3.66 milliseconds per image compared to 3.43 milliseconds. The resource usage of the SBF was also slightly 
higher, with an average of 433 MiB of RAM compared to 432 MiB for the WBF. These differences are negligible, 
indicating that the SBF is as computationally efficient as the WBF, with only minimal increases in runtime and 
resource usage, while significantly improving defect detection performance.
Conclusion
This paper evaluated the performance of modern object detection methods for detecting internal defects in 
EBSM components and introduced an model ensemble method that harnesses the strengths of various detection 
approaches to achieve optimal performance. The following conclusions were drawn: 
	1.	 Modern object detection methods show significant potential in detecting internal defects in EBSM compo­
nents. Among the evaluated models, Sparse R-CNN exhibited the best overall performance, achieving the 
highest mAP and mAR across all defect categories. It excelled in both precision and recall for pores and small 
defects, while also delivering the highest recall rates for cracks and lack of fusion. YOLOv5 demonstrated 
strong precision in detecting cracks and lack of fusion. For medium and large defects, the YOLOs outper­
formed others in precision, while Sparse R-CNN continued to excel in recall. DETR-based methods, which 
often require large datasets to perform optimally, did not match the levels of success seen in general object 
detection tasks. Additionally, Faster R-CNN, though historically significant, lagged in performance due to its 
relatively older model architecture.
	2.	 The model ensemble method, Selective Box Fusion (SBF), proposed in this study utilizes a voting strategy to 
select valid predictions and employs a weighted fusion approach to integrate bounding boxes from multiple 
models. The SBF effectively combines the strengths of individual methods, leading to performance improve­
ments of 1% to 3% across various evaluation metrics.
